---\\\\n2025-03-27\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni Technical Report\\\\nQwen Team\\\\nhttps://huggingface.co/Qwen\\\\nhttps://modelscope.cn/organization/qwen\\\\nhttps://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2.5-Omni\\\\nAbstract\\\\nIn this report, we present Qwen2.5-Omni, an end-to-end multimodal model designed to\\\\nperceive diverse modalities, including text, images, audio, and video, while simultane-\\\\nously generating text and natural speech responses in a streaming manner. To enable\\\\nthe streaming of multimodal information inputs, both audio and visual encoders utilize\\\\na block-wise processing approach. This strategy effectively decouples the handling of\\\\nlong sequences of multimodal data, assigning the perceptual responsibilities to the mul-\\\\ntimodal encoder and entrusting the modeling of extended sequences to a large language\\\\nmodel. Such a division of labor enhances the fusion of different modalities via the shared\\\\nattention mechanism. To synchronize the timestamps of video inputs with audio, we\\\\norganize the audio and video sequentially in an interleaved manner and propose a novel\\\\nposition embedding approach, named TMRoPE (Time-aligned Multimodal RoPE). To\\\\nconcurrently generate text and speech while avoiding interference between the two\\\\nmodalities, we propose Thinker-Talker architecture. In this framework, Thinker func-\\\\ntions as a large language model tasked with text generation, while Talker is a dual-track\\\\nautoregressive model that directly utilizes the hidden representations from the Thinker to\\\\nproduce audio tokens as output. Both the Thinker and Talker models are designed to be\\\\ntrained and inferred in an end-to-end manner. For decoding audio tokens in a streaming\\\\nmanner, we introduce a sliding-window DiT that restricts the receptive field, aiming\\\\nto reduce the initial package delay. Qwen2.5-Omni is comparable with similarly sized\\\\nQwen2.5-VL and outperforms Qwen2-Audio. Furthermore, Qwen2.5-Omni achieves\\\\nstate-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks like Omni-Bench. Notably,\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni ’s performance in end-to-end speech instruction following is comparable\\\\nto its capabilities with text inputs, as evidenced by benchmarks such as MMLU and\\\\nGSM8K. As for speech generation, Qwen2.5-Omni’s streaming Talker outperforms most\\\\nexisting streaming and non-streaming alternatives in robustness and naturalness.\\\\nFigure 1: Qwen2.5-Omni is a unified end-to-end model capable of processing multiple modalities, such\\\\nas text, audio, image and video, and generating real-time text or speech response. Based on these\\\\nfeatures, Qwen2.5-Omni supports a wide range of tasks, including but not limited to voice dialogue,\\\\nvideo dialogue, and video reasoning.\\\\n1\\\\narXiv:2503.20215v1  [cs.CL]  26 Mar 2025\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 2 ---\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nIn daily life, humans are capable of simultaneously perceiving the visual and auditory information\\\\naround them. After processing this information through the brain, they express feedback through\\\\nwriting, vocalization, or using tools (and physical actions), thereby engaging in information exchange\\\\nwith various organisms in the world and exhibiting intelligence. In recent years, general artificial\\\\nintelligence has become increasingly visible, largely due to advancements in Large Language Models\\\\n(LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023; 2024; Gemini Team, 2024; Anthropic, 2023a;b; 2024; Bai et al.,\\\\n2023a; Yang et al., 2024a; Touvron et al., 2023a;b; Dubey et al., 2024a). These models, trained on vast\\\\namounts of textual data, represent high-level discrete representation created by humans, showcasing\\\\nthe ability to solve complex problems and learn rapidly. Furthermore, in the realm of understanding,\\\\nLanguage-Audio-Language Models (LALMs) (OpenAI, 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2023b; 2024b)\\\\nand Language-Visual-Language Models (LVLMs) (Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Dai et al., 2023; Zhu\\\\net al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023b; OpenAI., 2023;\\\\nGemini Team, 2024) have helped LLMs to further extend auditory and visual capabilities in an end-to-end\\\\nmanner. However, efficiently unifying all these different understanding modalities in an end-to-end\\\\nfashion, utilizing as much data as possible, and providing responses in both text and speech streams akin\\\\nto human communication still presents a significant challenge.\\\\nThe development of a unified and intelligent omni-model requires careful consideration of several key\\\\nfactors. First, it is crucial to implement a systematic method for the joint training of various modalities,\\\\nincluding text, images, videos, and audio, to foster mutual enhancement among them. This alignment\\\\nis particularly important for video content, where synchronization of the temporal aspects of audio\\\\nand visual signals is necessary. Second, it is essential to manage potential interference among outputs\\\\nfrom different modalities, ensuring that the training processes for outputs such as text and voice tokens\\\\ndo not disrupt each other. Finally, there is a need to explore architectural designs that enable real-\\\\ntime understanding of multimodal information and allow for efficient audio output streaming, thereby\\\\nreducing initial latency.\\\\nIn this report, we introduce Qwen2.5-Omni, a unified single model capable of processing multiple\\\\nmodalities and generating text and natural speech responses simultaneously in a streaming format. To\\\\ntackle the first challenge, we propose a novel position embedding approach, named TMRoPE (Time-\\\\naligned Multimodal RoPE). We organize these audio and video frames in an interleaved structure to\\\\nrepresent video sequences in time order. For the second challenge, we present Thinker-Talker architecture,\\\\nwherein Thinker is tasked with text generation while the Talker focuses on generating streaming speech\\\\ntokens. Talker receives high-level representations directly from Thinker. This design is inspired by the\\\\nway humans utilize different organs to produce various signals, which are simultaneously coordinated\\\\nthrough the same neural networks. As a result, Thinker-Talker architecture is end-to-end jointly trained,\\\\nwith each component dedicated to generating distinct signals. To address the challenges associated with\\\\nstreaming and to facilitate the pre-filling necessary for real-time comprehension of multimodal signals,\\\\nwe propose modifications to all multimodal encoders by adopting a block-wise streaming processing\\\\napproach. In order to support streaming speech generation, we implement a dual-track autoregressive\\\\nmodel that generates speech tokens, alongside a DiT model which converts these tokens into waveforms,\\\\nthereby enabling streaming audio generation and minimizing initial latency. This design aims to enable\\\\nthe model to process multimodal information in real-time and effectively perform pre-filling, thereby\\\\nenabling the concurrent generation of text and speech signals.\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni is comparable with the similarly sized Qwen2.5-VL (Wang et al., 2024c) and outperforms\\\\nQwen2-Audio (Chu et al., 2024b) in image and audio capabilities respectively. Furthermore, Qwen2.5-\\\\nOmni achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal benchmarks such as OmniBench (Li et al.,\\\\n2024b) and AV-Odyssey Bench (Gong et al., 2024). Notably, Qwen2.5-Omni’s performance in end-to-\\\\nend speech instruction following is comparable to its capabilities with text inputs, as evidenced by\\\\nbenchmarks such as MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). As for speech\\\\ngeneration, Qwen2.5-Omni achieves 1.42%, 2.33% and 6.54% WER on seed-tts-eval (Anastassiou et al.,\\\\n2024) test-zh, test-en and test-hard set respectively, outperforming MaskGCT (Wang et al., 2024e) and\\\\nCosyVoice 2 (Du et al., 2024).\\\\nThe key features of Qwen2.5-Omni can be summarized as:\\\\n• We introduce Qwen2.5-Omni, a unified model that can perceive all modalities and simultaneously\\\\ngenerate text and natural speech responses in a streaming fashion.\\\\n• We present a novel positional embedding algorithm, termed TMRoPE, which explicitly incorpo-\\\\nrates temporal information for synchronizing audio and video.\\\\n• We propose the Thinker-Talker Architecture to facilitate real-time comprehension and speech\\\\ngeneration.\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\n• Qwen2.5-Omni demonstrates strong performance across all modalities when benchmarked\\\\nagainst similarly sized single-modality models. It significantly enhances the capability of follow-\\\\ning voice commands, achieving performance levels comparable to pure text input. For tasks that\\\\ninvolve integrating multiple modalities, such as those evaluated in OmniBench (Li et al., 2024b),\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, Qwen2.5-Omni achieves strong\\\\nperformance on seed-tts-eval (Anastassiou et al., 2024), demonstrating robust speech generation\\\\nabilities.\\\\n2\\\\nArchitecture\\\\nFigure 2: The overview of Qwen2.5-Omni. Qwen2.5-Omni adpots the Thinker-Talker architecture.\\\\nThinker is tasked with text generation while Talker focuses on generating streaming speech tokens by\\\\nreceives high-level representations directly from Thinker.\\\\n2.1\\\\nOverview\\\\nAs shown in Figure 2, Qwen2.5-Omni employs Thinker-Talker architecture. Thinker functions like\\\\na brain, responsible for processing and understanding inputs from text, audio and video modalities,\\\\ngenerating high-level representations and corresponding text. Talker operates like a human mouth,\\\\ntaking in the high-level representations and text produced by the Thinker in a streaming manner, and\\\\noutputting discrete tokens of speech fluidly. Thinker is a Transformer decoder, accompanied by encoders\\\\nfor audio and image that facilitate information extraction. In contrast, Talker is designed as a dual-track\\\\nautoregressive Transformer Decoder architecture, motivated by Mini-Omni (Xie & Wu, 2024). During\\\\nboth training and inference, Talker directly receives high-dimensional representations from Thinker and\\\\nshares all of Thinker’s historical context information. Consequently, the entire architecture operates as a\\\\ncohesive single model, enabling end-to-end training and inference.\\\\nIn the following sections, we first introduce how Qwen2.5-Omni perceives various input signals and\\\\npresent our proposed novel positional encoding algorithm, TMRoPE. Subsequently, the details of text\\\\nand speech generation are presented. Finally, we highlight the improvements made in the understanding\\\\nand generation modules to facilitate efficient streaming inference.\\\\n3\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\n2.2\\\\nPerceivation\\\\nFigure 3: An illustration of Time-aligned Multimodal RoPE (TMRoPE).\\\\nText, Audio, Image and Video (w/o Audio).\\\\nThinker processes text, audio, images, and video (without\\\\nthe audio track) by converting them into a series of hidden representations for input. For tokenizing\\\\ntext, we use Qwen’s tokenizer (Yang et al., 2024a), which applies byte-level byte-pair encoding with\\\\na vocabulary comprising 151,643 regular tokens. Regarding audio input and audio from videos, we\\\\nresample it to a frequency of 16kHz and transform the raw waveform into a 128-channel mel-spectrogram\\\\nwith a window size of 25ms and a hop size of 10ms. We adopt the audio encoder from Qwen2-Audio (Chu\\\\net al., 2024b), to make each frame of audio representation roughly corresponds to a 40ms segment of\\\\nthe original audio signal. Furthermore, we employ the vision encoder from Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al.,\\\\n2025), which is based on the Vision Transformer (ViT) model with approximately 675 million parameters,\\\\nenabling it to effectively handle both image and video inputs. The vision encoder employs a mixed\\\\ntraining regimen incorporating both image and video data, ensuring proficiency in image understanding\\\\nand video comprehension. To preserve video information as completely as possible while adapting to the\\\\naudio sampling rate, we sample the video using a dynamic frame rate. Additionally, for consistency, each\\\\nimage is treated as two identical frames.\\\\nVideo and TMRoPE.\\\\nWe propose a time-interleaving algorithm for audio and video, along with a novel\\\\nposition encoding approach. As shown in Figure 3, TMRoPE encodes the 3-D positional information\\\\nof multimodal inputs, which is Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (M-RoPE) (Bai et al., 2023b)\\\\nwith absolute temporal positions. This is achieved by deconstructing the original rotary embedding\\\\ninto three components: temporal, height, and width. For text inputs, these components utilize identical\\\\nposition IDs, making M-RoPE functionally equivalent to 1D-RoPE. Similarly, for audio inputs, we also\\\\nuse identical position IDs and introduce absolute temporal position encoding, with one temporal ID\\\\ncorresponding to 40ms.\\\\nWhen processing images, the temporal IDs of each visual token remain constant, while distinct IDs are\\\\nassigned to the height and width components based on the token’s position in the image. When the\\\\ninput is video with audio, the audio is still encoded with identical position IDs for every 40ms per frame,\\\\nand the video is treated as a series of images with temporal ID increments for each frame, while the\\\\nheight and width components follow the same ID assignment pattern as images. Since the frame rate\\\\nin video is not fixed, we dynamically adjust the temporal IDs between frames based on the actual time\\\\ncorresponding to each frame to ensure that one temporal ID corresponds to 40ms. In scenarios where the\\\\nmodel’s input encompasses multiple modalities, position numbering for each modality is initialized by\\\\nincrementing the maximum position ID of the preceding modality by one. TMRoPE enhances positional\\\\ninformation modeling, maximizing the integration of various modalities, enabling Qwen2.5-Omni to\\\\nsimultaneously understand and analyze information from multiple modalities.\\\\nAfter incorporating positional information into each modality, we arrange the representations in order. To\\\\nenable the model to receive both visual and auditory information simultaneously, as shown in Figure 3,\\\\nwe have a special design for video with audio called the time-interleaving method, which segments the\\\\nrepresentation in the video with audio into chunks every 2 seconds according to the actual time. We\\\\nthen arrange the visual representation at the front and the audio representation at the back within the 2\\\\nseconds, interleaving the representations of the video with audio.\\\\n2.3\\\\nGeneration\\\\nText.\\\\nText is generated directly by Thinker. The logic of text generation is fundamentally the same as\\\\nthat employed by widely used LLMs, which generate text through autoregressive sampling based on the\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 5 ---\\\\nprobability distribution over the vocabulary. The generation process may incorporate techniques such as\\\\nrepetition penalty and top-p sampling to enhance its diversity.\\\\nSpeech.\\\\nTalker receives both high-level representations and embeddings of the text tokens sampled by\\\\nThinker. The integration of high-dimensional representations and discrete sampling tokens is essential in\\\\nthis context. As a streaming algorithm, voice generation must anticipate the content’s tone and attitude\\\\nbefore the entire text is fully generated. The high-dimensional representations provided by Thinker\\\\nimplicitly convey this information, enabling a more natural streaming generation process. Furthermore,\\\\nThinker’s representations primarily express semantic similarity in the representational space rather than\\\\nphonetic similarity. Consequently, even phonetically distinct words may have very similar high-level\\\\nrepresentations, necessitating the input of sampled discrete tokens to eliminate such uncertainty.\\\\nWe designed an efficient speech codec named qwen-tts-tokenizer. qwen-tts-tokenizer efficiently represents\\\\nkey information of speech and can be decoded to speech streamingly through a causal audio decoder.\\\\nAfter receiving the information, Talker starts to autoregressively generate audio tokens and text tokens.\\\\nThe generation of speech does not require word-level and timestamp-level alignment with the text. This\\\\nsignificantly simplifies the requirements for training data and the inference process.\\\\n2.4\\\\nDesigns for Streaming\\\\nIn the context of streaming audio and video interactions, the initial packet latency is a critical indicator of\\\\nthe system’s streaming performance. This latency is influenced by several factors: 1) the delay caused\\\\nby the processing of multimodal information inputs; 2) the latency from the moment the first text\\\\ninput is received until the first voice token is output; 3) the delay in converting the first segment of\\\\nspeech into audio; and 4) the inherent latency of the architecture itself, which is related to model size,\\\\ncomputational FLOPs, and other factors. This paper will subsequently discuss the algorithmic and\\\\narchitectural improvements made to reduce these latencies across these four dimensions.\\\\nSupport Prefilling.\\\\nChunked-prefills is a mechanism widely used in modern inference framework. To\\\\nsupport it in modalities interation, we modified the audio and visual encoders to support block-wise\\\\nattention along the temporal dimension. Specifically, the audio encoder is changed from full attention\\\\nover the entire audio to performing attention in blocks of 2 seconds each. The vision encoder utilizes flash\\\\nattention for efficient training and inference with a simple MLP layer that merges adjacent 2×2 tokens\\\\ninto a single token. The patch size is set to 14, which allows images of different resolutions to be packed\\\\ninto a sequence.\\\\nStreaming Codec Generation.\\\\nTo facilitate the streaming of audio, especially for extended sequences,\\\\nwe propose a sliding window block attention mechanism that restricts the current token’s access to a\\\\nlimited context. Specifically, we utilize a Flow-Matching (Lipman et al.) DiT model. The input code is\\\\ntransformed into a mel-spectrogram using Flow-Matching, followed by a modified BigVGAN (Lee et al.)\\\\nto reconstruct the generated mel-spectrogram back into the waveform.\\\\nFigure 4: An illustration of sliding window block attention mechanism in DiT for codec to wav generation.\\\\nAs shown in Figure 4, to generate waveforms from code, we group adjacent codes into blocks and use\\\\nthese for our attention mask. We limit the DiT’s receptive field to 4 blocks, including a lookback of 2\\\\nblocks and a lookahead of 1 block. During decoding, we generate the mel-spectrum in chunks using Flow\\\\nMatching, ensuring that each code chunk has access to the necessary contextual blocks. This approach\\\\nenhances the quality of streaming outputs by maintaining contextual information. We also use this\\\\nchunk-by-chunk method for BigVGAN’s fixed receptive field to facilitate streaming waveform generation\\\\n5\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\n3\\\\nPre-training\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni consists of three training stages. In the first stage, we lock the LLM parameters and focus\\\\nexclusively on training the vision encoder and audio encoder, utilizing a vast corpus of audio-text and\\\\nimage-text pairs to enhance semantic understanding within the LLM. In the second stage, we unfreeze\\\\nall parameters and train with a wider range of multimodal data for more comprehensive learning. In\\\\nthe final stage, we use data with a sequence length of 32k to enhance the model’s ability to understand\\\\ncomplex long-sequence data.\\\\nThe model is pre-trained on a diverse dataset that includes various types such as image-text, video-text,\\\\nvideo-audio, audio-text and text corpus. We replace the hierarchical tags with the natural language\\\\nprompts following Qwen2-Audio (Chu et al., 2024a), which can improve better generalization ability and\\\\nbetter instruction following ability.\\\\nDuring the initial pre-training phase, the LLM component of Qwen2.5-Omni is initialized using the\\\\nparameters from Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024b), while the vision encoder is the same as Qwen2.5-VL, and\\\\nthe audio encoder is initialized with the Whisper-large-v3 (Radford et al., 2023). The two encoders are\\\\ntrained separately on the fixed LLM, with both initially focusing on training their respective adapters\\\\nbefore training the encoders. This foundational training is crucial in equipping the model with a robust\\\\nunderstanding of core visual-textual and audio-textual correlations and alignments.\\\\nThe second phase of pre-training marks a significant advancement by incorporating an additional 800\\\\nbillion tokens of image and video related data, 300 billion tokens of audio related data, and 100 billion\\\\ntokens of video with audio related data. This phase introduces a larger volume of mixed multimodal data\\\\nand a wider variety of tasks, which enhances the interaction and deepens the understanding between\\\\nauditory, visual, and textual information. The inclusion of multimodal, multitask datasets is crucial for\\\\ndeveloping the model’s ability to handle multiple tasks and modalities simultaneously, a vital capability\\\\nfor managing complex real-world datasets. Moreover, pure text data plays an essential role in maintaining\\\\nand improving language proficiency.\\\\nTo improve training efficiency, we limited the maximum token length to 8192 tokens in the previous\\\\nstages. Then, we incorporat long audio and long video data and extend the original text, audio, image,\\\\nand video data to 32,768 tokens for training. Experimental results indicate that our data shows significant\\\\nimprovement in supporting long sequence data\\\\n4\\\\nPost-training\\\\n4.1\\\\nData Format\\\\nThe Dataset Format Example of ChatML\\\\n<|im_start|>user\\\\n<|vision_start|>Video.mp4 [Two people are talking in the video]<|vision_end|>What are the\\\\npeople in the video saying?<|im_end|>\\\\n<|im_start|>assistant\\\\nBoth pictures are of SpongeBob SquarePants.The person in the red clothes says, \\\\\\\"Hello, how’s\\\\nthe weather today?\\\\\\\" The person in the black clothes responds, \\\\\\\"Hello, the weather is quite nice\\\\ntoday.\\\\\\\"<|im_end|>\\\\n<|im_start|>user\\\\n<|vision_start|>Video.mp4 [A person in the video is saying, \\\\\\\"Please describe the person in front\\\\nof you.\\\\\\\"]<|vision_end|><|im_end|>\\\\n<|im_start|>assistant\\\\nThe person in front of you is wearing glasses and a brown jacket over a blue shirt. The\\\\nlighting in the room is warm and cozy.<|im_end|>\\\\n4.2\\\\nThinker\\\\nDuring the post-training phase, we employ instruction-following data with ChatML (OpenAI, 2022)\\\\nformat for instruction-finetuning. Our dataset incorporates pure text-based dialogue data, visual-modality\\\\nconversation data, audio-modality conversation data and mix-modality conversation data.\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\n4.3\\\\nTalker\\\\nWe introduced a three-stage training process for Talker, allowing Qwen2.5-Omni to generate text and\\\\nspeech responses simultaneously. In the first stage, we train Talker to learn context continuation. The\\\\nsecond stage utilized DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) to enhance the stability of speech generation. In the third\\\\nstage, we applied multi-speaker instruction fine-tuning to improve the naturalness and controllability of\\\\nthe speech responses.\\\\nDuring the In-Context Learning (ICL) training phase, in addition to utilizing text supervision similar\\\\nto that of Thinker, we perform a speech continuation task through next-token prediction, leveraging\\\\nan extensive dataset of dialogues that incorporate multimodal contexts and spoken responses. Talker\\\\nlearns to establish a monotonic mapping from semantic representation to speech, while also acquiring\\\\nthe ability to express speech with diverse attributes that are contextually appropriate, such as prosody,\\\\nemotion, and accent. Additionally, we implement timbre disentanglement techniques to prevent the\\\\nmodel from associating specific voices with infrequent textual patterns.\\\\nLDPO(Pθ; Pref) = −E(x,yw,yl)∼D\\\\n\\\\u0014\\\\nlog σ\\\\n\\\\u0012\\\\nβ log Pθ(yw | x)\\\\nPref(yw | x) −β log Pθ(yl | x)\\\\nPref(yl | x)\\\\n\\\\u0013\\\\u0015\\\\n.\\\\n(1)\\\\nTo broaden the coverage of speakers and scenarios, the pretraining data inevitably contains label noise and\\\\npronunciation errors, leading to model hallucinations. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a reinforcement\\\\nlearning phase to improve the stability of speech generation. Specifically, for each request and response\\\\ntext paired with the reference speech, we build a dataset D with the triplet data (x, yw, yl), where x is\\\\nthe input sequence with input text, and yw and yl are the good and bad generated speech sequences\\\\nrespectively. We rank these samples based on their reward scores associated with word error rate (WER)\\\\nand the punctuation pause error rate.\\\\nLastly, we performed speaker fine-tuning on the aforementioned base model, enabling Talker to adopt\\\\nspecific voices and improve its naturalness.\\\\n5\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nWe conduct comprehensive evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni. Due to the lack of\\\\nrelevant assessments, the evaluation of speech generation focuses primarily speech generation given\\\\ntexts, similarity to text-to-speech (TTS), on two aspects: Zero-shot and Single-Speaker speech generation\\\\ncapabilities.\\\\n• Zero-Shot Speech Generation We assessed the content consistency (WER) and speaker similarity\\\\n(SIM) of our model in zero-shot speech generation on SEED (Anastassiou et al., 2024).\\\\n• Single-Speaker Speech Generation We assessed the stability of our speaker fine-tuned model\\\\non the SEED (Anastassiou et al., 2024), and evaluated the subjective naturalness (NMOS) of the\\\\ngenerated speech on a self-created dataset.\\\\n5.2.1\\\\nEvaluation of Zero-Shot Speech Generation.\\\\nWe compared the Qwen2.5-Omni with state-of-the-art zero-shot TTS systems. As shown in Table 9,\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni demonstrates highly competitive performance, highlighting its robust speech under-\\\\nstanding and generation capabilities developed through in-context learning (ICL). Additionally, after\\\\nreinforcement learning (RL) optimization, Qwen2.5-Omni showed significant improvements in genera-\\\\ntion stability, with marked reductions in attention misalignment, pronunciation errors, and inappropriate\\\\npauses on the challenging test-hard dataset.\\\\n5.2.2\\\\nEvaluation of Single-Speaker Speech Generation.\\\\nWe compared the Qwen2.5-Omni model before and after speaker fine-tuning, as well as with human\\\\nrecordings. As shown in Table 10, the speaker-finetuned Qwen2.5-Omni more precisely captured the\\\\nnuanced prosodic styles of the target speakers while preserving the foundational stability provided by\\\\nthe base model, achieving performance that approaches human-level quality across both subjective and\\\\nobjective metrics.\\\\n6\\\\nConclusion\\\\nQwen2.5-Omni is a unified model designed to understand and generate multiple modalities, including\\\\ntext and real-time speech. To enhance video integration, we’ve introduced a new positional embedding\\\\nmethod called TMRoPE, which aligns audio and video timing. Our Thinker-Talker framework supports\\\\nreal-time speech generation while minimizing interference across different modalities. Additionally, we\\\\nemploy techniques such as block-wise audio/vision encoding and a sliding window mechanism for code-\\\\nto-wav generation. This innovative model excels in complex audio-visual interactions and emotional\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 13 ---\\\\nTable 9: Zero-Shot Speech Moon-\\\\nshine is based on an encoder-decoder transformer\\\\narchitecture and employs Rotary Position Em-\\\\nbedding (RoPE) instead of traditional absolute\\\\nposition embeddings. The model is trained on\\\\nspeech segments of various lengths, but with-\\\\nout using zero-padding, leading to greater ef-\\\\nficiency for the encoder during inference time.\\\\nWhen benchmarked against OpenAI’s Whisper\\\\ntiny.en, Moonshine Tiny demonstrates a 5x re-\\\\nduction in compute requirements for transcribing\\\\na 10-second speech segment while incurring no in-\\\\ncrease in word error rates across standard evalua-\\\\ntion datasets. These results highlight Moonshine’s\\\\npotential for real-time and resource-constrained\\\\napplications.\\\\n1. Introduction\\\\nReal-time automatic speech recognition (ASR) is essential\\\\nfor many applications, including live transcription during\\\\npresentations, accessibility tools for individuals with hear-\\\\ning impairments, and voice command processing for conver-\\\\nsational interfaces in smart devices and wearables. These\\\\napplications often run directly on low-cost hardware, where\\\\nstrict resource constraints and a lack of internet connectivity\\\\nintroduce unique technical challenges that are not present in\\\\nother ASR domains.\\\\nThe introduction of OpenAI’s Whisper has led to a signifi-\\\\ncant improvement in the accuracy of general-purpose ASR\\\\nsystems (Radford et al., 2022). However, one of the pri-\\\\nmary challenges in applications of on-device ASR is the\\\\nneed to minimize latency—the time delay between a spoken\\\\nutterance and the corresponding text appearing, e.g., on a\\\\nlive transcription display—without losing accuracy. During\\\\n.\\\\nCorrespondence\\\\nto:\\\\nManjunath\\\\nKudlur\\\\n<keve-\\\\nman@usefulsensors.com>.\\\\nour development of one such application—a Caption Box\\\\nbuilt to provide rapid, accurate, and private offline transcrip-\\\\ntion of English speech—we found that current models are\\\\nill-suited to the task. When deployed on a low-cost ARM-\\\\nbased processor, we noticed that even the smallest Whisper\\\\ntiny.en model had a firm lower latency bound of 500\\\\nmilliseconds, irrespective of the duration of audio. User\\\\nfeedback indicated that this level of latency failed to provide\\\\na smooth and responsive user experience, which motivated\\\\nus to investigate deeper.\\\\nWhisper, which is based on an encoder-decoder transformer\\\\narchitecture, processes fixed-length audio sequences in 30-\\\\nsecond chunks regardless of the actual speech content of\\\\nthe audio. This means that shorter audio sequences require\\\\npadding with zeros to meet the length requirement, resulting\\\\nin a constant computational overhead in the encoder. While\\\\nthe decoder’s processing time is proportional to the length\\\\nof the utterance, the constant overhead of fixed-length en-\\\\ncoding places a firm lower bound to latency—e.g., the 500\\\\nmilliseconds we identified during our own testing with the\\\\nCaption Box. Our initial attempts to remove this bottle-\\\\nneck involved fine-tuning and distilling 1 Whisper models\\\\nto handle variable-length sequences in the encoder, utilizing\\\\nopen audio datasets. However, these open datasets proved\\\\ninsufficient to surpass Whisper’s Word Error Rate (WER).\\\\nRecognizing the limits of available data and the opportunity\\\\nto leverage recent advancements in model architectures, we\\\\nopted to develop and train new models from scratch.\\\\nOur first task was to better quantify the bottleneck imposed\\\\nby Whisper’s fixed-length encoder. In an empirical test,\\\\nwe compared the GFLOPS (i.e., billion floating-point op-\\\\nerations) needed for processing 30 seconds of zero-padded\\\\naudio to the GFLOPS that would be required to instead pro-\\\\ncess only a < 30 second subset of the same audio—i.e., we\\\\nmeasured the potential for speed-ups if Whisper instead had\\\\na variable-length encoder. Our results (Figure 1) showed\\\\npotential for a 35x speed-up in the best case, and nearly a\\\\n5x speed-up overall. Clearly, improvements to Whisper’s\\\\narchitecture could yield lightweight, low-latency speech-to-\\\\n1Hence the name Moonshine. Moonshine models are de-\\\\nsigned to match Whisper’s accuracy while optimizing com-\\\\nputational efficiency by eliminating zero-padding require-\\\\nments, instead scaling processing demands proportionally\\\\nto audio input length. Section 5 concludes.\\\\n2. Issues with fixed sequence length encoder\\\\nWhisper models use absolute position embeddings in both\\\\nthe encoder and decoder. The encoder in particular uses\\\\nsinusoidal position embeddings of shape [1500, dim],\\\\nwhere dim is the transformer encoder’s dimension. The\\\\nstandard inference code provided by OpenAI zero-pads the\\\\ninput audio to an exact 30-second segment before passing it\\\\ndown to the model. Audio feature generation and 2 convolu-\\\\ntion layers convert this audio segment to a [1500, dim]\\\\nvector sequence that gets added to the sinusoidal position\\\\nembedding. The left-most column of Figure 2 illustrates\\\\nthis mechanism.\\\\nRequiring an exact 30-second segment causes the encoder\\\\nto incur a fixed computation cost, no matter the duration\\\\nof actual speech in the audio segment. However, since\\\\nWhisper’s model architecture is an off-the-shelf, variable-\\\\nlength sequence-to-sequence transformer, zero-padding is\\\\nnot strictly necessary. An audio segment that is shorter\\\\nthan 30 seconds can indeed be processed through the\\\\nmodel’s frontend to yield a [seq_length, dim] vector\\\\nsequence where seq_length <= 1500.\\\\nThere are several options for adding the position embedding\\\\nto a variable-length audio input. We compared the default\\\\nimplementation in OpenAI’s Whisper inference code (i.e.,\\\\nusing zero-padding to form 30-second segments) with two\\\\nother options, as illustrated in the center and right-most\\\\ncolumns of Figure 2—namely, using the prefix and the\\\\nsuffix of the position embedding. We computed the WER\\\\nfor the tiny.en model using these two options on the\\\\ntest.clean split of the Librispeech dataset. This split\\\\nhas 2620 examples, 9 of which are more than 30 seconds in\\\\nlength. We ignore these 9 examples in this evaluation. We\\\\nuse a beam size of 5, so as to not suffer the pitfalls of greedy\\\\ndecoding such as repetitions. With the standard inference\\\\ncode provided by OpenAI, we get a WER of 5.21%. When\\\\nthe input is not zero-padded, however, we get worse results.\\\\nWhen using only a prefix of the position embedding, the\\\\ntiny.en model has a WER of 107.38%. We notice a\\\\nlot of repetitions towards the end of the transcription, even\\\\nwith the beam search. When instead using the suffix of\\\\nthe position embedding, the accuracy degradation is not as\\\\ndramatic, producing a WER of 18.45%—still more than\\\\nthree times worse than the baseline.\\\\nThese results indicate that the OpenAI Whisper models\\\\nare trained with examples that are all exactly 30 seconds\\\\nlong. The models indeed produce high quality transcrip-\\\\ntions for long-form audio. However, the fixed computation\\\\nbudget needed for their encoder makes them inefficient for\\\\nlow-latency applications, such as live transcription. Since\\\\nthe audio segments in these applications tend to be short\\\\nand/or vary in length, our effort to train models optimized\\\\nfor variable-length sequences is well-motivated.\\\\n3. Approach\\\\nThis section describes Moonshine’s model architecture be-\\\\nfore detailing our data collection, preprocessing, and model\\\\ntraining process.\\\\n3.1. Model architecture\\\\nMoonshine is an off-the-shelf encoder-decoder Transformer\\\\n(Vaswani et al., 2017) model. The input is an audio signal\\\\nsampled at 16,000 Hz. We do not use any hand-engineering\\\\n(e.g., Mel spectrograms) to extract audio features. Instead,\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nMoonshine: Speech Recognition for Live Transcription and Voice Commands\\\\n3\\\\nx + positional_embedding[:,:]\\\\nx + positional_embedding[:x.shape[1],:]\\\\nx + positional_embedding[-x.shape[1]:,:]\\\\n+\\\\n+\\\\n+\\\\n5.21% WER\\\\n107.38% WER\\\\n18.45% WER\\\\nZero-Padded\\\\nTruncated (Prefix)\\\\nTruncated (Suffix)\\\\nFigure 2. Variations of absolute position embeddings usage and the corresponding WER produced by Whisper tiny.en (test.clean\\\\nsplit of the Librispeech dataset). Simply adapting Whisper’s inference code to avoid encoding of fixed-length audio (as in the center and\\\\nright-most columns) introduces significant increases in WER, motivating our development of new models with variable-length encoding.\\\\nthe input is processed by a short stem of 3 convolution layers\\\\nwith strides 64, 3, and 2 respectively. The filter widths,\\\\nnumber of channels and activation functions are shown in\\\\nFigure 3. These set of strides compress the input by a\\\\nfactor of 384x. Note that in the Whisper model, the input is\\\\ncompressed by 320x—firstly 160x in the Mel spectogram\\\\ncomputation, then by a further 2x in the convolution stem.\\\\nWe use Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2023)\\\\nat each layer of the encoder and decoder. The original vocabulary size is\\\\n32000; we add 768 special tokens for future extensions.\\\\n3.2. Training data collection & preprocessing\\\\nWe train Moonshine on a combination of 90K hours\\\\nfrom open ASR datasets and over 100K hours from own\\\\ninternally-prepared dataset, totalling around 200K hours.\\\\nFrom open datasets, we use Common Voice 16.1 (Ardila\\\\net al., 2020), the AMI corpus (Carletta et al., 2005), Gi-\\\\ngaSpeech (Chen et al., 2021), LibriSpeech (Panayotov\\\\net al., 2015), the English subset of multilingual Lib-\\\\nriSpeech (Pratap et al., 2020), and People’s Speech (Galvez\\\\net al., 2021). We then augment this training corpus with\\\\ndata that we collect from openly-available sources on the\\\\nweb. We discuss preparation methods for our self-collected\\\\ndata in the following.\\\\nPreprocessing noisily-labeled speech.\\\\nMany speech\\\\nsources available on the web have subtitles or captions avail-\\\\nable, which can serve as labels. However, captions tend be\\\\nnoisy—they may be manually-generated and thus contain\\\\ntext that is orthogonal to the audio content, or they may\\\\ncontain the names of speakers or verbal descriptions of non-\\\\nspeech content. In cases where a manually-generated but\\\\npossibly-unreliable caption is available, we use a heuristic\\\\nprocess to filter out low-quality instances. First, we lower-\\\\ncase and normalize the caption text, removing or replacing,\\\\ne.g., ambiguous unicode characters, emoji, and punctuation.\\\\nWe then use Whisper large v3 to generate a pseudo-label\\\\nof the audio content, applying the same text normalization\\\\nto this pseudo-label as we do the caption. Finally, we com-\\\\npute a normalized Levenshtein distance (between [0.0, 1.0],\\\\nwhere 0.0 is identical and 1.0 is orthogonal) between the\\\\nnormalized caption and the pseudo-label, filtering out labels\\\\nwith a distance above a threshold. This allows us to treat the\\\\nhuman-generated labels in captions as ground truth without\\\\nintroducing excessive noise. After filtering out noisy labels,\\\\nwe prepare the remaining text by applying standardized\\\\npunctuation and capitalization.\\\\nPreprocessing unlabeled speech. The majority of speech\\\\navailable on the web is unlabeled. In these cases, we lever-\\\\nage the Whisper large v3 model to generate training labels\\\\nfor our lighter-weight Moonshine model. The risk inherent\\\\nin training one model on another model’s outputs is that\\\\nthe new model learns the old model’s errors. From inspec-\\\\ntion, we noted that the majority of hallucinated outputs from\\\\nWhisper large v3 occurred below a predictable value of the\\\\naverage log probability of the output. We thus mitigate\\\\nthe risk of introducing hallucination and other noise in the\\\\ntraining set by filtering out instances with an average log\\\\nprobability below this threshold. During this process, we\\\\nbenefited from speed-ups provided by batched inference in\\\\nthe WhisperX implementation (Bain et al., 2023).\\\\nControlling instance duration. We assemble successive\\\\nspeech segments into longer training instances, such that\\\\nthe resulting instance duration is ∈[4, 30] seconds with no\\\\nmore than 2 seconds between successive segments. For\\\\nour manually-captioned data sources, we use timestamped\\\\nsegments provided by a subtitle file (e.g., an .srt file); for\\\\nour pseudo-labeled audio, we use the timestamps output by\\\\nWhisper. Upon combining this data with open datasets, the\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\nMoonshine: Speech Recognition for Live Transcription and Voice Commands\\\\n4\\\\nRoPE\\\\nself-attention\\\\nFFN + GELU\\\\nFFN + SwiGLU\\\\nRoPE\\\\nself-attention\\\\ncross-attention\\\\n...\\\\nConv1D\\\\ntanh\\\\nkernel size: 127\\\\nstride: 64\\\\nConv1D\\\\nGELU\\\\nkernel size: 7\\\\nstride: 3\\\\n...\\\\nConv1D\\\\nkernel size: 3\\\\nstride: 2\\\\nEncoder\\\\nBlocks\\\\nDecoder\\\\nBlocks\\\\nnext-token\\\\nprediction\\\\nBPE\\\\nGELU\\\\nFigure 3. Discussion & Conclusion\\\\nWe briefly discuss limitations before concluding the paper\\\\nin this section.\\\\nArchitectures and optimizers.\\\\nAs in any research of\\\\nthis kind, many variations of model architecture could be\\\\nexplored. Likewise, recent advancements in optimizers—\\\\nparticularly Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018) and SOAP (Vyas\\\\net al., 2024)—show promise for improving WERs in our\\\\narchitecture. Conducting an ablation study on these model\\\\narchitectures and training methods would significantly en-\\\\nhance the community’s understanding of the models’ limi-\\\\ntations. However, due to resource constraints, particularly\\\\nlimited affordability of GPUs, such studies are beyond the\\\\nscope of this paper. Consequently, we chose our architec-\\\\nture and optimizer based on the authors’ experience and a\\\\nthorough review of relevant literature.\\\\nGeneralization to shorter audio segments. The relatively\\\\nlow performance that we observed on the Earnings22 dataset\\\\nmotivates collection of more data representative of this case,\\\\nand investigation of training techniques to introduce more\\\\ncontextual information in the model. This will likely im-\\\\nprove model performance with no changes to architecture.\\\\nIn this paper we introduced Moonshine, a family of\\\\nlightweight ASR models optimized for low latency, on-\\\\ndevice speech-to-text applications. We outlined our model\\\\narchitecture, data collection and preprocessing procedures,\\\\nand training. We benchmarked Moonshine against two\\\\nOpenAI Whisper models—tiny.en and base.en—\\\\nshowing that their Moonshine counterparts provide up to 3x\\\\nreductions in latency scaled to the duration of input audio.\\\\nOur work opens the door for new applications of real-time\\\\nASR in live transcription, accessibility technologies, and\\\\nsmart devices.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nMoonshine: Speech Recognition for Live Transcription and Voice Commands\\\\n7\\\\n6. Introduction\\\\nProgress in speech recognition has been energized by the\\\\ndevelopment of unsupervised pre-training techniques exem-\\\\npliﬁed by Wav2Vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020). Since these\\\\nmethods learn directly from raw audio without the need for\\\\nhuman labels, they can productively use large datasets of un-\\\\nlabeled speech and have been quickly scaled up to 1,000,000\\\\nhours of training data (Zhang et al., 2021), far more than the\\\\n1,000 or so hours typical of an academic supervised dataset.\\\\nWhen ﬁne-tuned on standard benchmarks, this approach\\\\nhas improved the state of the art, especially in a low-data\\\\nsetting.\\\\nThese pre-trained audio encoders learn high-quality repre-\\\\nsentations of speech, but because they are purely unsuper-\\\\nvised they lack an equivalently performant decoder mapping\\\\nthose representations to usable outputs, necessitating a ﬁne-\\\\ntuning stage in order to actually perform a task such as\\\\nspeech recognition1. This unfortunately limits their use-\\\\nfulness and impact as ﬁne-tuning can still be a complex\\\\nprocess requiring a skilled practitioner. There is an addi-\\\\ntional risk with requiring ﬁne-tuning. (2021) is an exciting exception - having devel-\\\\noped a fully unsupervised speech recognition system\\\\nmethods are exceedingly adept at ﬁnding patterns within a\\\\ntraining dataset which boost performance on held-out data\\\\nfrom the same dataset. However, some of these patterns are\\\\nbrittle and spurious and don’t generalize to other datasets\\\\nand distributions. In a particularly disturbing example, Rad-\\\\nford et al. A model that achieves “superhuman” per-\\\\nformance when trained on a dataset can still make many\\\\nbasic errors when evaluated on another, possibly precisely\\\\nbecause it is exploiting those dataset-speciﬁc quirks that\\\\nhumans are oblivious to (Geirhos et al., 2020).\\\\nThis suggests that while unsupervised pre-training has im-\\\\nproved the quality of audio encoders dramatically, the lack\\\\nof an equivalently high-quality pre-trained decoder, com-\\\\nbined with a recommended protocol of dataset-speciﬁc ﬁne-\\\\ntuning, is a crucial weakness which limits their usefulness\\\\nand robustness. The goal of a speech recognition system\\\\nshould be to work reliably “out of the box” in a broad range\\\\nof environments without requiring supervised ﬁne-tuning of\\\\na decoder for every deployment distribution.\\\\nAs demonstrated by Narayanan et al. (2018), Likhomanenko\\\\net al. (2020), and Chan et al. (2021) speech recognition sys-\\\\ntems that are pre-trained in a supervised fashion across many\\\\ndatasets/domains exhibit higher robustness and generalize\\\\nmuch more effectively to held-out datasets than models\\\\ntrained on a single source. These works achieve this by\\\\ncombining as many existing high-quality speech recogni-\\\\ntion datasets as possible. However, there is still only a\\\\nmoderate amount of this data easily available. SpeechStew\\\\n(Chan et al., 2021) mixes together 7 pre-existing datasets\\\\ntotalling 5,140 hours of supervision. While not insigniﬁ-\\\\ncant, this is still tiny compared to the previously mentioned\\\\n1,000,000 hours of unlabeled speech data utilized in Zhang\\\\net al. (2021).\\\\nRecognizing the limiting size of existing high-quality super-\\\\nvised datasets, recent efforts have created larger datasets for\\\\nspeech recognition. By relaxing the requirement of gold-\\\\nstandard human-validated transcripts, Chen et al. (2021) and\\\\nGalvez et al. (2021) make use of sophisticated automated\\\\narXiv:2212.04356v1  [eess.AS]  6 Dec 2022\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 2 ---\\\\nRobust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision\\\\n2\\\\npipelines to scale weakly supervised speech recognition\\\\nto 10,000 and 30,000 hours of noisier training data. This\\\\ntrade-off between quality and quantity is often the right\\\\ncall. Although understudied so far for speech recognition,\\\\nrecent work in computer vision has demonstrated that mov-\\\\ning beyond gold-standard crowdsourced datasets such as\\\\nImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015) to much larger but\\\\nweakly supervised datasets signiﬁcantly improves the ro-\\\\nbustness and generalization of models (Mahajan et al., 2018;\\\\nKolesnikov et al., 2020).\\\\nYet these new datasets are only a few times larger than the\\\\nsum of existing high-quality datasets and still much smaller\\\\nthan prior unsupervised work. In this work we close that\\\\ngap, scaling weakly supervised speech recognition the next\\\\norder of magnitude to 680,000 hours of labeled audio data.\\\\nWe call our approach Whisper2. We demonstrate models\\\\ntrained at this scale transfer well to existing datasets zero-\\\\nshot, removing the need for any dataset-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning\\\\nto achieve high-quality results.\\\\nIn addition to scale, our work also focuses on broaden-\\\\ning the scope of weakly supervised pre-training beyond\\\\nEnglish-only speech recognition to be both multilingual and\\\\nmultitask. Of those 680,000 hours of audio, 117,000 hours\\\\ncover 96 other languages. The dataset also includes 125,000\\\\nhours of X→en translation data. We ﬁnd that for sufﬁciently\\\\nlarge models there is no drawback and even beneﬁts to joint\\\\nmultilingual and multitask training.\\\\nOur work suggests that simple scaling of weakly supervised\\\\npre-training has been underappreciated so far for speech\\\\nrecognition. We achieve these results without the need for\\\\nthe self-supervision or self-training techniques that have\\\\nbeen a mainstay of recent large-scale speech recognition\\\\nwork. To serve as a foundation for further research on robust\\\\nspeech recognition, we release inference code and models at\\\\nthe following URL: https://github.com/openai/\\\\nwhisper.\\\\n2. Approach\\\\n2.1. Data Processing\\\\nFollowing the trend of recent work leveraging web-scale\\\\ntext from the internet for training machine learning systems,\\\\nwe take a minimalist approach to data pre-processing. In\\\\ncontrast to a lot of work on speech recognition, we train\\\\nWhisper models to predict the raw text of transcripts without\\\\nany signiﬁcant standardization, relying on the expressive-\\\\nness of sequence-to-sequence models to learn to map be-\\\\ntween utterances and their transcribed form. This simpliﬁes\\\\n2If an acronym or basis for the name is desired, WSPSR stand-\\\\ning for Web-scale Supervised Pretraining for Speech Recognition\\\\ncan be used.\\\\nthe speech recognition pipeline since it removes the need\\\\nfor a separate inverse text normalization step in order to\\\\nproduce naturalistic transcriptions.\\\\nWe construct the dataset from audio that is paired with tran-\\\\nscripts on the Internet. This results in a very diverse dataset\\\\ncovering a broad distribution of audio from many different\\\\nenvironments, recording setups, speakers, and languages.\\\\nWhile diversity in audio quality can help train a model to be\\\\nrobust, diversity in transcript quality is not similarly bene-\\\\nﬁcial. Initial inspection showed a large amount of subpar\\\\ntranscripts in the raw dataset. To address this, we developed\\\\nseveral automated ﬁltering methods to improve transcript\\\\nquality.\\\\nMany transcripts on the internet are not actually human-\\\\ngenerated but the output of existing ASR systems. Recent\\\\nresearch has shown that training on datasets of mixed human\\\\nand machine-generated data can signiﬁcantly impair the per-\\\\nformance of translation systems (Ghorbani et al., 2021). In\\\\norder to avoid learning “transcript-ese”, we developed many\\\\nheuristics to detect and remove machine-generated tran-\\\\nscripts from the training dataset. Many existing ASR sys-\\\\ntems output only a limited subset of written language which\\\\nremoves or normalizes away aspects that are difﬁcult to pre-\\\\ndict from only audio signals such as complex punctuation\\\\n(exclamation points, commas, and question marks), format-\\\\nting whitespace such as paragraphs, or stylistic aspects such\\\\nas capitalization. An all-uppercase or all-lowercase tran-\\\\nscript is very unlikely to be human generated. While many\\\\nASR systems include some level of inverse text normaliza-\\\\ntion, it is often simple or rule-based and still detectable from\\\\nother unhandled aspects such as never including commas.\\\\nWe also use an audio language detector, which was created\\\\nby ﬁne-tuning a prototype model trained on a prototype ver-\\\\nsion of the dataset on VoxLingua107 (Valk & Alum¨ae, 2021)\\\\nto ensure that the spoken language matches the language of\\\\nthe transcript according to CLD2. If the two do not match,\\\\nwe don’t include the (audio, transcript) pair as a speech\\\\nrecognition training example in the dataset. We make an\\\\nexception if the transcript language is English and add these\\\\npairs to the dataset as X→en speech translation training\\\\nexamples instead. We use fuzzy de-duping of transcript\\\\ntexts to reduce the amount of duplication and automatically\\\\ngenerated content in the training dataset.\\\\nWe break audio ﬁles into 30-second segments paired with\\\\nthe subset of the transcript that occurs within that time\\\\nsegment. We train on all audio, including segments where\\\\nthere is no speech (though with sub-sampled probability)\\\\nand use these segments as training data for voice activity\\\\ndetection.\\\\nFor an additional ﬁltering pass, after training an initial model\\\\nwe aggregated information about its error rate on training\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nRobust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision\\\\n3\\\\ndata sources and performed manual inspection of these data\\\\nsources sorting by a combination of both high error rate and\\\\ndata source size in order to identify and remove low-quality\\\\nones efﬁciently. This inspection showed a large amount of\\\\nonly partially transcribed or poorly aligned/misaligned tran-\\\\nscripts as well as remaining low-quality machine-generated\\\\ncaptions that ﬁltering heuristics did not detect.\\\\nTo avoid contamination, we perform de-duplication at a tran-\\\\nscript level between the training dataset and the evaluation\\\\ndatasets we thought were at higher risk of overlap, namely\\\\nTED-LIUM 3 (Hernandez et al., 2018).\\\\n2.2. Model\\\\nSince the focus of our work is on studying the capabilities\\\\nof large-scale supervised pre-training for speech recogni-\\\\ntion, we use an off-the-shelf architecture to avoid confound-\\\\ning our ﬁndings with model improvements. We chose an\\\\nencoder-decoder Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as this\\\\narchitecture has been well validated to scale reliably. All\\\\naudio is re-sampled to 16,000 Hz, and an 80-channel log-\\\\nmagnitude Mel spectrogram representation is computed on\\\\n25-millisecond windows with a stride of 10 milliseconds.\\\\nFor feature normalization, we globally scale the input to\\\\nbe between -1 and 1 with approximately zero mean across\\\\nthe pre-training dataset. The encoder processes this input\\\\nrepresentation with a small stem consisting of two convolu-\\\\ntion layers with a ﬁlter width of 3 and the GELU activation\\\\nfunction (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016) where the second\\\\nconvolution layer has a stride of two. Sinusoidal position\\\\nembeddings are then added to the output of the stem after\\\\nwhich the encoder Transformer blocks are applied. The\\\\ntransformer uses pre-activation residual blocks (Child et al.,\\\\n2019), and a ﬁnal layer normalization is applied to the en-\\\\ncoder output. The decoder uses learned position embeddings\\\\nand tied input-output token representations (Press & Wolf,\\\\n2017). The encoder and decoder have the same width and\\\\nnumber of transformer blocks. Figure 1 summarizes the\\\\nmodel architecture.\\\\nWe use the same byte-level BPE text tokenizer used in GPT-\\\\n2 (Sennrich et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2019) for the English-\\\\nonly models and reﬁt the vocabulary (but keep the same size)\\\\nfor the multilingual models to avoid excessive fragmenta-\\\\ntion on other languages since the GPT-2 BPE vocabulary is\\\\nEnglish only.\\\\n2.3. Multitask Format\\\\nAlthough predicting which words were spoken in a given\\\\naudio snippet is a core part of the full speech recognition\\\\nproblem and extensively studied in research, it is not the\\\\nonly part. A fully featured speech recognition system can\\\\ninvolve many additional components such as voice activ-\\\\nity detection, speaker diarization, and inverse text normal-\\\\nization. These components are often handled separately,\\\\nresulting in a relatively complex system around the core\\\\nspeech recognition model. To reduce this complexity, we\\\\nwould like to have a single model perform the entire speech\\\\nprocessing pipeline, not just the core recognition part. An\\\\nimportant consideration here is the interface for the model.\\\\nThere are many different tasks that can be performed on\\\\nthe same input audio signal: transcription, translation, voice\\\\nactivity detection, alignment, and language identiﬁcation\\\\nare some examples.\\\\nFor this kind of one-to-many mapping to work with a single\\\\nmodel, some form of task speciﬁcation is necessary. We use\\\\na simple format to specify all tasks and conditioning infor-\\\\nmation as a sequence of input tokens to the decoder. Since\\\\nour decoder is an audio-conditional language model, we also\\\\ntrain it to condition on the history of text of the transcript in\\\\nthe hope that it will learn to use longer-range text context\\\\nto resolve ambiguous audio. Speciﬁcally, with some proba-\\\\nbility we add the transcript text preceding the current audio\\\\nsegment to the decoder’s context. We indicate the beginning\\\\nof prediction with a <|startoftranscript|> token.\\\\nFirst, we predict the language being spoken which is repre-\\\\nsented by a unique token for each language in our training\\\\nset (99 total). These language targets are sourced from the\\\\naforementioned VoxLingua107 model. In the case where\\\\nthere is no speech in an audio segment, the model is trained\\\\nto predict a <|nospeech|> token indicating this. The\\\\nnext token speciﬁes the task (either transcription or trans-\\\\nlation) with an <|transcribe|> or <|translate|>\\\\ntoken. After this, we specify whether to predict timestamps\\\\nor not by including a <|notimestamps|> token for that\\\\ncase. At this point, the task and desired format is fully\\\\nspeciﬁed, and the output begins. For timestamp predic-\\\\ntion, we predict time relative to the current audio segment,\\\\nquantizing all times to the nearest 20 milliseconds which\\\\nmatches the native time resolution of Whisper models, and\\\\nadd additional tokens to our vocabulary for each of these.\\\\nWe interleave their prediction with the caption tokens: the\\\\nstart time token is predicted before each caption’s text, and\\\\nthe end time token is predicted after. When a ﬁnal tran-\\\\nscript segment is only partially included in the current 30-\\\\nsecond audio chunk, we predict only its start time token\\\\nfor the segment when in timestamp mode, to indicate that\\\\nthe subsequent decoding should be performed on an au-\\\\ndio window aligned with that time, otherwise we truncate\\\\nthe audio to not include the segment. Lastly, we add a\\\\n<|endoftranscript|> token. We only mask out the\\\\ntraining loss over the previous context text, and train the\\\\nmodel to predict all other tokens. Please see Figure 1 for an\\\\noverview of our format and training setup.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\nRobust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision\\\\n4\\\\n⋯\\\\n⋯\\\\n2 × Conv1D + GELU\\\\n⋮\\\\ncross attention\\\\nLog-Mel Spectrogram\\\\n~\\\\nSOT\\\\nEN\\\\nTRANS-\\\\nCRIBE\\\\n0.0\\\\nThe quick\\\\nTokens in Multitask Training Format\\\\nTransformer\\\\nEncoder Blocks\\\\nTransformer\\\\nDecoder Blocks\\\\nEN\\\\n0.0\\\\nThe quick brown\\\\n⋮\\\\n⋮\\\\nnext-token\\\\nprediction\\\\nSinusoidal\\\\nPositional\\\\nEncoding\\\\nLearned\\\\nPositional\\\\nEncoding\\\\nMultitask training data (680k hours)\\\\nSequence-to-sequence learning\\\\nMultitask training format\\\\nEnglish transcription\\\\nAny-to-English speech translation\\\\nNon-English transcription\\\\nNo speech\\\\n🗣️  “Ask not what your country can do for ⋯”\\\\n📝  Ask not what your country can do for ⋯\\\\n🗣️  “El rápido zorro marrón salta sobre ⋯”\\\\n📝  The quick brown fox jumps over ⋯\\\\n🗣️ “언덕 위에 올라 내려다보면 너무나 넓고 넓은 ⋯”\\\\n📝  언덕 위에 올라 내려다보면 너무나 넓고 넓은 ⋯\\\\n🔊 (background music playing)\\\\n📝  ∅\\\\nPREV\\\\nspecial\\\\ntokens\\\\ntext\\\\ntokens\\\\ntimestamp\\\\ntokens\\\\nSTART OF\\\\nTRANSCRIPT\\\\nLANGUAGE\\\\nTAG\\\\nNO\\\\nSPEECH\\\\nEOT\\\\nTRANSCRIBE\\\\nTRANSLATE\\\\nbegin\\\\ntime\\\\nNO\\\\nTIMESTAMPS\\\\n⋯\\\\nend\\\\ntime\\\\ntext tokens\\\\nbegin\\\\ntime\\\\nend\\\\ntime\\\\ntext tokens\\\\ntext tokens\\\\nVoice activity\\\\ndetection\\\\n(VAD)\\\\nCustom vocabulary /\\\\nprompting\\\\nTime-aligned transcription\\\\nText-only transcription\\\\n(allows dataset-specific fine-tuning)\\\\nX → English\\\\nTranslation \\\\nprevious\\\\ntext tokens\\\\nX → X\\\\nTranscription \\\\nLanguage\\\\nidentification\\\\nMLP\\\\nself attention\\\\nMLP\\\\nself attention\\\\nMLP\\\\nself attention\\\\nMLP\\\\ncross attention\\\\nself attention\\\\nMLP\\\\ncross attention\\\\nself attention\\\\nMLP\\\\ncross attention\\\\nself attention\\\\nTRANS-\\\\nCRIBE\\\\nFigure 1. Training Details\\\\nWe train a suite of models of various sizes in order to study\\\\nthe scaling properties of Whisper. Please see Table 1 for an\\\\noverview. We train with data parallelism across accelerators\\\\nusing FP16 with dynamic loss scaling and activation check-\\\\npointing (Griewank & Walther, 2000; Chen et al., 2016).\\\\nModels were trained with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter,\\\\n2017) and gradient norm clipping (Pascanu et al., 2013)\\\\nwith a linear learning rate decay to zero after a warmup over\\\\nthe ﬁrst 2048 updates. Due to only\\\\ntraining for a few epochs, over-ﬁtting is not a large concern,\\\\nand we do not use any data augmentation or regularization\\\\nand instead rely on the diversity contained within such a\\\\nlarge dataset to encourage generalization and robustness.\\\\nPlease see Appendix F for full training hyperparameters.3\\\\nDuring early development and evaluation we observed that\\\\nWhisper models had a tendency to transcribe plausible but\\\\nalmost always incorrect guesses for the names of speakers.\\\\nThis happens because many transcripts in the pre-training\\\\ndataset include the name of the person who is speaking,\\\\nencouraging the model to try to predict them, but this infor-\\\\nmation is only rarely inferable from only the most recent 30\\\\n3After the original release of Whisper, we trained an additional\\\\nLarge model (denoted V2) for 2.5X more epochs while adding\\\\nSpecAugment (Park et al., 2019), Stochastic Depth (Huang et al.,\\\\n2016), and BPE Dropout (Provilkov et al., 2019) for regularization.\\\\nReported results have been updated to this improved model unless\\\\notherwise speciﬁed.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 5 ---\\\\nRobust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision\\\\n5\\\\nModel\\\\nLayers\\\\nWidth\\\\nHeads\\\\nParameters\\\\nTiny\\\\n4\\\\n384\\\\n6\\\\n39M\\\\nBase\\\\n6\\\\n512\\\\n8\\\\n74M\\\\nSmall\\\\n12\\\\n768\\\\n12\\\\n244M\\\\nMedium\\\\n24\\\\n1024\\\\n16\\\\n769M\\\\nLarge\\\\n32\\\\n1280\\\\n20\\\\n1550M\\\\nTable 1. To avoid this, we ﬁne-tune Whis-\\\\nper models brieﬂy on the subset of transcripts that do not\\\\ninclude speaker annotations which removes this behavior.\\\\n3. Experiments\\\\n3.1. Zero-shot Evaluation\\\\nThe goal of Whisper is to develop a single robust speech\\\\nprocessing system that works reliably without the need for\\\\ndataset speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning to achieve high-quality results\\\\non speciﬁc distributions. To study this capability, we re-\\\\nuse a wide set of existing speech processing datasets to\\\\ncheck whether Whisper is able to generalize well across\\\\ndomains, tasks, and languages. Instead of using the standard\\\\nevaluation protocol for these datasets, which include both\\\\na train and test split, we evaluate Whisper in a zero-shot\\\\nsetting without using any of the training data for each of\\\\nthese datasets so that we are measuring broad generalization.\\\\n3.2. Evaluation Metrics\\\\nSpeech recognition research typically evaluates and com-\\\\npares systems based on the word error rate (WER) metric.\\\\nHowever, WER, which is based on string edit distance, pe-\\\\nnalizes all differences between the model’s output and the\\\\nreference transcript including innocuous differences in tran-\\\\nscript style. As a result, systems that output transcripts that\\\\nwould be judged as correct by humans can still have a large\\\\nWER due to minor formatting differences. While this poses\\\\na problem for all transcribers, it is particularly acute for\\\\nzero-shot models like Whisper, which do not observe any\\\\nexamples of speciﬁc datasets transcript formats.\\\\nThis is not a novel observation; the development of evalua-\\\\ntion metrics that better correlate with human judgement is an\\\\nactive area of research, and while there are some promising\\\\nmethods, none have seen widespread adoption for speech\\\\nrecognition yet. We opt to address this problem with ex-\\\\ntensive standardization of text before the WER calculation\\\\nto minimize penalization of non-semantic differences. Our\\\\ntext normalizer was developed through iterative manual in-\\\\nspection to identify common patterns where naive WER\\\\npenalized Whisper models for an innocuous difference. Ap-\\\\npendix C includes full details. For several datasets, we\\\\nobserve WER drops of up to 50 percent usually due to a\\\\nquirk such as a dataset’s reference transcripts seperating\\\\ncontractions from words with whitespace. We caution this\\\\ndevelopment procedure comes at a risk of overﬁtting to the\\\\ntranscription style of Whisper models which we investigate\\\\nin Section 4.4. We are releasing the code for our text nor-\\\\nmalizer to allow for easy comparison and to help others\\\\nstudy the performance of speech recognition systems in\\\\nout-of-distribution settings.\\\\n3.3. English Speech Recognition\\\\nIn 2015, Deep Speech 2 (Amodei et al., 2015) reported\\\\na speech recognition system matched human-level perfor-\\\\nmance when transcribing the LibriSpeech test-clean split.\\\\nAs part of their analysis they concluded: “Given this result,\\\\nwe suspect that there is little room for a generic speech sys-\\\\ntem to further improve on clean read speech without further\\\\ndomain adaptation.” Yet seven years later the SOTA WER\\\\non LibriSpeech test-clean has dropped another 73% from\\\\ntheir 5.3% to 1.4% (Zhang et al., 2021), far below their re-\\\\nported human-level error rate of 5.8%. Despite this massive\\\\nand unanticipated further improvement in performance on\\\\nheld-out but in-distribution data, speech recognition mod-\\\\nels trained on LibriSpeech remain far above human error\\\\nrates when used in other settings. What explains this gap\\\\nbetween reportedly superhuman performance in-distribution\\\\nand subhuman performance out-of-distribution?\\\\nWe suspect a large part of this gap between human and\\\\nmachine behavior is due to conﬂating different capabilities\\\\nbeing measured by human and machine performance on\\\\na test set. This claim may seem confusing at ﬁrst; if both\\\\nhumans and machines are taking the same test, how can it be\\\\nthat different skills are being tested? The difference arises\\\\nnot in the testing but in how they trained for it. Humans are\\\\noften asked to perform a task given little to no supervision\\\\non the speciﬁc data distribution being studied. Thus human\\\\nperformance is a measure of out-of-distribution generaliza-\\\\ntion. But machine learning models are usually evaluated\\\\nafter training on a large amount of supervision from the\\\\nevaluation distribution, meaning that machine performance\\\\nis instead a measure of in-distribution generalization. While\\\\nboth humans and machines are being evaluated on the same\\\\ntest data, two quite different abilities are being measured\\\\ndue to a difference in train data.\\\\nWhisper models, which are trained on a broad and diverse\\\\ndistribution of audio and evaluated in a zero-shot setting,\\\\ncould potentially match human behavior much better than\\\\nexisting systems. To study whether this is the case (or\\\\nwhether the difference between machine and human per-\\\\nformance is due to yet-to-be-understood factors) we can\\\\ncompare Whisper models with both human performance\\\\nand standard ﬁne-tuned machine learning models and check\\\\nwhich they more closely match.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\nRobust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision\\\\n6\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\n6\\\\n7\\\\n8\\\\nWER on LibriSpeech dev-clean (%)\\\\n0\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\n50\\\\nAverage WER on [Common Voice, CHiME-6, TED-LIUM] (%)\\\\nSupervised LibriSpeech models\\\\nZero-shot Whisper models\\\\nZero-shot Human (Alec)\\\\nIdeal robustness (y = x)\\\\nFigure 2. The estimated robustness\\\\nfrontier of zero-shot Whisper models, however, includes the 95%\\\\nconﬁdence interval for this particular human.\\\\nTo quantify this difference, we examine both overall ro-\\\\nbustness, that is average performance across many distribu-\\\\ntions/datasets, and effective robustness, introduced by Taori\\\\net al. (2020), which measures the difference in expected\\\\nperformance between a reference dataset, which is usually\\\\nin-distribution, and one or more out-of-distribution datasets.\\\\nA model with high effective robustness does better than\\\\nexpected on out-of-distribution datasets as a function of its\\\\nperformance on the reference dataset and approaches the\\\\nideal of equal performance on all datasets. For our analy-\\\\nsis, we use LibriSpeech as the reference dataset due to its\\\\ncentral role in modern speech recognition research and the\\\\navailability of many released models trained on it, which\\\\nallows for characterizing robustness behaviors. We use a\\\\nsuite of 12 other academic speech recognition datasets to\\\\nstudy out-of-distribution behaviors. Full details about these\\\\ndatasets can be found in Appendix A.\\\\nOur main ﬁndings are summarized in Figure 2 and Table 2.\\\\nAlthough the best zero-shot Whisper model has a relatively\\\\nunremarkable LibriSpeech clean-test WER of 2.5, which\\\\nis roughly the performance of modern supervised baseline\\\\nor the mid-2019 state of the art, zero-shot Whisper models\\\\nhave very different robustness properties than supervised\\\\nLibriSpeech models and out-perform all benchmarked Lib-\\\\nriSpeech models by large amounts on other datasets. Long-form Transcription\\\\nWhisper models are trained on 30-second audio chunks and\\\\ncannot consume longer audio inputs at once. This is not a\\\\nproblem with most academic datasets comprised of short\\\\nutterances but presents challenges in real-world applications\\\\nwhich often require transcribing minutes- or hours-long au-\\\\ndio. We developed a strategy to perform buffered transcrip-\\\\ntion of long audio by consecutively transcribing 30-second\\\\nsegments of audio and shifting the window according to the\\\\ntimestamps predicted by the model. We observed that it\\\\nis crucial to have beam search and temperature scheduling\\\\nbased on the repetitiveness and the log probability of the\\\\nmodel predictions in order to reliably transcribe long audio.\\\\nThe full procedure is described in Section 4.5.\\\\nWe evaluate the long-form transcription performance on\\\\nseven datasets consisting of speech recordings of various\\\\nlengths and recording conditions, to cover as diverse a data\\\\ndistribution as possible. Full details about the long-form datasets can\\\\nbe found in Appendix A.\\\\nWe compare the performance with open-source models as\\\\nwell as 4 commercial ASR services. Comparison with Human Performance\\\\nBecause of ambiguous or indistinct speech as well as la-\\\\nbeling errors, there are different levels of irreducible error\\\\nin each dataset, and with WER metrics from ASR systems\\\\nalone it is difﬁcult to make sense of how much room for\\\\nimprovement exists in each dataset. Figure 7 shows the distribution\\\\nof per-example WERs and aggregate WER across the 25\\\\nrecordings, where the computer-assisted service has the\\\\nlowest aggregate WER that is 1.15% point better than Whis-\\\\nper’s, and the pure-human performance is only a fraction\\\\nof a percentage point better than Whisper’s. These results\\\\nindicate that Whisper’s English ASR performance is not\\\\nperfect but very close to human-level accuracy.\\\\n4. Analysis and Ablations\\\\n4.1. A re-\\\\nlated concern is that as capacity and compute spent training\\\\non the dataset increases, models may learn to exploit the\\\\nWhisper\\\\nA\\\\nB\\\\nC\\\\nD\\\\nE\\\\nF\\\\nG\\\\nH\\\\nI\\\\n ASR \\\\n          \\\\n human transcription \\\\n \\\\n          computer-assisted\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\n25\\\\n30\\\\nWord Error Rate (%)\\\\nFigure 7. Multitask and Multilingual Transfer\\\\nA potential concern with jointly training a single model\\\\non many tasks and languages is the possibility of negative\\\\ntransfer where interference between the learning of several\\\\ntasks results in performance worse than would be achieved\\\\nby training on only a single task or language. We adjust for\\\\nthe amount of FLOPs spent training on the task of English\\\\nspeech recognition as only 65% of compute is spent on this\\\\ntask in a joint training setup; analysis would otherwise be\\\\nconfounded by under-training on the task when compared\\\\nto a same-sized English-only model.\\\\nOur results visualized in Figure 9 show that for small models\\\\ntrained with moderate amounts of compute, there is indeed\\\\nnegative transfer between tasks and languages: joint mod-\\\\nels underperform English-only models trained for the same\\\\namount of compute.
